As grad student currently publishing, I feel as though I almost have to take a Devil's advocate approach with this. This problem is very similar to the Not In My Backyard (NIMBY) one when it comes to nuclear waste (strange parallel, I know). The idea is as follows:

  • Nuclear energy seems like a good idea that I can get behind (hypothetically)
  • Nuclear energy will produce nuclear waste, which I don't like
  • We should push for nuclear energy! As for the nuclear waste, we can store it anywhere...just not in my backyard/city/state/etc.

Replicating experiments is a vital step in improving the scientific body of knowledge. However, there are actually disincentives for doing this. First, and foremost, is that you will not get funding for this research. Research is currently about novel ideas, and trying to convince your peers (much less government organizations such as the NSF) that repeating the experiment is necessary is very hard (almost impossible) in terms of funding. The best you can hope for is build upon that body of knowledge, which involves looking at previous research with a critical eye.

In addition, you will be a social pariah within the community if you do not tread carefully. You're essentially calling someone and saying, "hey, you didn't do this right." Worse yet, unless you do what I said before (i.e. building upon that body of knowledge), it looks like you're saying "Hey, I haven't thought of a solution but I know you're wrong." It's not a great way to make friends and/or get a job after graduation.

The article suggests a number of changes, but they're extremely weak. It's essentially saying "hey, the world should change and I should get a pony." The world needs garbage men and sewage workers to make it run just as it needs people to seek out and replicate these findings. But changing the system requires changing the way people think about it. In a world where one 'bad' study can often mean the end of your academic career, these suggestions don't take into the account the actual people who would be performing this research. Who wants to be a poor grad student, shunned by both the outside world AND academia with even bleaker job prospects because your research pisses off people in your field?
